name: Adaptive Structuration Theory
summary: A theory of how groups actively reshape technology as they use it, so that outcomes flow not from the tool alone but from how people appropriate it.
originator: Gerardine DeSanctis and Marshall Scott Poole (building on Anthony Giddens)

name: Agenda-Setting Theory
summary: The news may not tell us what to think, but it is strikingly successful at telling us what to think about.
originator: Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw

name: Altercasting
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: A persuader nudges others into a social role that, once accepted, makes the desired behavior feel like simply being who they are.
originator: Eugene A. Weinstein and Paul Deutschberger (later extended as an influence tactic by Anthony R. Pratkanis)

name: Argumentation Theory
summary: The study of how people justify claims to one another through reasons, treating everyday argument as a structured, reason-giving practice rather than formal logic.
originator: Stephen Toulmin, with later development by Frans van Eemeren and Rob Grootendorst (pragma-dialectics)

name: Attraction-Selection-Attrition Framework
summary: Organizations slowly become collections of similar people, because a shared cycle of who is drawn in, who is hired, and who leaves quietly grinds them toward sameness.
originator: Benjamin Schneider

name: Attribution Theory
summary: The theory of how people act as everyday detectives, inferring the causes behind their own and others' behavior, and how those causal stories shape what they feel, expect, and do next.
originator: Fritz Heider, with major elaborations by Harold Kelley and Bernard Weiner (and Edward Jones with Keith Davis on correspondent inference)

name: Classical Rhetoric
summary: The founding Western account of persuasion, which holds that an orator moves an audience through credibility, emotion, and reasoning, fitted to the moment.
key_terms: The five canons (invention, arrangement, style, memory, delivery)
originator: Aristotle, building on the Greek Sophists and Plato, and later systematized by Roman teachers Cicero and Quintilian
year: 4th century BCE (Aristotle's Rhetoric, c. 350 BCE), with the broader tradition spanning the 5th century BCE through the 1st century CE

name: Cognitive Dissonance Theory
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: When our beliefs and our actions clash, the discomfort itself becomes a motive, and we revise the attitude rather than admit the mismatch.
originator: Leon Festinger

name: Computer Mediated Communication
summary: An umbrella account of how people make and exchange meaning through networked devices, and how stripping away the body changes the message.
originator: Early field-shaping work by Starr Roxanne Hiltz and Murray Turoff, and by Sara Kiesler, Jane Siegel, and Timothy McGuire; the communication-theoretic line was later anchored by Joseph Walther

name: Contextual Design
summary: A field-grounded method for designing information systems by watching people work in their own context, then turning what is observed into shared models that drive design.
originator: Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt
year: 1998 (developed from contextual inquiry work in the late 1980s and early 1990s)

name: Coordinated Management of Meaning
summary: A practical theory holding that people do not merely describe social reality through talk, they build it together, coordinating meanings turn by turn so that conversation literally makes the worlds we live in.
originator: W. Barnett Pearce and Vernon E. Cronen

name: Cultivation Theory
summary: The more time people spend living in the world of television, the more they come to see real life through its recurring lessons.
originator: George Gerbner (with Larry Gross and colleagues at the Annenberg School)
year: 1968 (Cultural Indicators Project); core theory developed through the 1970s

name: Dependency Theory (Media System Dependency Theory)
summary: The more a person depends on media to meet their needs and make sense of the world, the more power those media hold to shape what they think, feel, and do.
originator: Sandra Ball-Rokeach and Melvin DeFleur

name: Diffusion of Innovations
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: A theory of how new ideas and technologies spread through a social system over time, sorting people into adopter categories and tracing the familiar S-shaped curve from first uptake to saturation.
key_terms: Adopter categories (innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards)
Perceived attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability)
originator: Everett M. Rogers (building on Bryce Ryan and Neal Gross)

name: Domestication (Domestication Theory)
summary: A theory of how households tame new media and technologies, turning strange commodities into familiar, meaningful parts of everyday life.
originator: Roger Silverstone, Eric Hirsch, and David Morley (with Leslie Haddon)
year: 1992 (developed from late-1980s work at Brunel University)

name: Elaboration Likelihood Model
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: Persuasion splits into two routes: deep thinking about the argument, or quick reliance on surface cues.
originator: Richard E. Petty & John T. Cacioppo

name: Expectancy Value Theory
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: A person's attitude toward something is the sum of what they believe about it multiplied by how much they value each of those beliefs.
originator: Martin Fishbein (with Icek Ajzen); media extension by Philip Palmgreen and J. D. Rayburn

name: Framing (Framing Theory)
summary: How a message is framed, which facts are made salient and which are left out, shapes how audiences define a problem and what they think should be done about it.
originator: Erving Goffman (sociological foundation); Robert Entman (communication paradigm)

name: Gatekeeping (Gatekeeping Theory)
summary: A small number of people and routines decide which of the world's countless events ever become news, controlling the gates through which information flows to the public.
originator: Kurt Lewin (coined the concept); David Manning White (first applied it to news selection); later systematized by Pamela J. Shoemaker and Timothy P. Vos
year: 1943-1950 (Lewin's channel studies in the 1940s; White's "Mr. Gates" study in 1950)

name: Health Belief Model
summary: A foundational account of why people do or do not take protective health action, built on what they believe about their risk, the stakes, and whether the recommended step is worth the trouble.
originator: Godfrey Hochbaum, Irwin Rosenstock, and Stephen Kegeles (U.S. Public Health Service); later refined by Marshall Becker and Nancy Janz

name: Hyperpersonal Model
summary: The claim that online communication can become more intimate and idealized than face-to-face contact, because people carefully craft how they appear and partners fill in the gaps with flattering assumptions.
originator: Joseph B. Walther

name: Hypodermic Needle Theory (Magic Bullet Theory)
summary: An early and now largely discredited view that mass media inject messages straight into a passive, uniform audience that absorbs them whole and acts accordingly.
originator: Associated with early mass-communication scholars of the propaganda era, notably Harold Lasswell (his 1927 Propaganda Technique in the World War is the work most often cited), though the labels were applied retrospectively by later critics rather than coined by any single author

name: Information Theory (Shannon-Weaver Model)
summary: The founding engineering model of communication, picturing a message as a signal that travels from a source through a channel to a destination while noise tries to corrupt it.
originator: Claude E. Shannon, with Warren Weaver

name: Knowledge Gap
summary: When a flood of information enters a community, the already advantaged learn from it faster than everyone else, so the gap in what people know tends to widen rather than close.
originator: Phillip J. Tichenor, George A. Donohue, and Clarice N. Olien (University of Minnesota)

name: Language Expectancy Theory
categories: Public Relations / Advertising, Marketing and Consumer Behavior
summary: Persuasion succeeds or fails depending on whether a message's language matches what the audience expects a speaker like this one to say.
key_terms: Message variables (fear appeals, opinionatedness, verbal aggression)
originator: Michael Burgoon and Gerald R. Miller
year: 1978 (roots in Burgoon, Jones, and Stewart, 1975; full formulation, Burgoon, 1995)

name: Media Richness Theory
summary: A channel's "richness," its capacity to carry feedback, cues, and personal nuance, should match how ambiguous the message is, or communication fails.
originator: Richard L. Daft and Robert H. Lengel

name: Medium Theory
summary: The form of a medium, not just its content, reshapes how we sense, know, and organize social life.
originator: Harold Innis and Marshall McLuhan (founders of the tradition); the term coined by Joshua Meyrowitz

name: Mental Models
summary: People build small internal working models of how systems behave, then run those models to predict, explain, and decide how to act.
originator: Kenneth Craik (concept, 1943); formalized by Philip Johnson-Laird; applied to human-computer interaction by Donald Norman

name: Minimalism
summary: A theory of instructional design holding that learners master technology faster when documentation is cut to the bone and built around real tasks rather than exhaustive explanation.
originator: John M. Carroll

name: Model of Text Comprehension
summary: A cognitive account of how readers turn strings of words into understanding, building meaning across three layers from the literal wording up to a mental picture of the situation the text describes.
originator: Walter Kintsch and Teun A. van Dijk

name: Modernization Theory
summary: The mid-century claim that exposure to mass media pulls traditional societies toward modern, Western attitudes and so drives national development.
originator: Daniel Lerner, with Wilbur Schramm and Everett Rogers

name: Network Theory and Analysis
summary: A way of seeing communication as the structure of who connects to whom, where the pattern of ties, not the traits of individuals, explains how information, influence, and resources flow.
originator: Jacob Moreno (sociometric roots); Mark Granovetter, Stanley Wasserman and Katherine Faust (methods); Peter Monge and Noshir Contractor (communication networks)

name: Online Disinhibition Effect
summary: People say and do things online that they would never say or do face to face, sometimes opening up with unusual warmth and sometimes turning cruel, because the screen loosens the ordinary brakes on behavior.
originator: John Suler

name: Parasocial Interaction
summary: The one-sided sense of friendship and intimacy that audiences feel toward media figures who do not know they exist.
originator: Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl

name: Priming (Priming Theory)
summary: By making certain issues mentally accessible, the media quietly hands audiences the yardstick they will use to judge leaders, events, and everything else.
originator: Shanto Iyengar, Mark Peters, and Donald Kinder

name: Protection Motivation Theory
summary: A model of how fear-based messages work, holding that people protect themselves only when they judge a threat to be serious and likely and believe a recommended response will work and is within their power.
originator: Ronald W. Rogers

name: Psycho-Linguistic Theory
summary: The study of how the mind produces, understands, stores, and acquires language, treating words and sentences as cognitive events rather than abstract grammar.
originator: Charles E. Osgood and Thomas A. Sebeok (with George A. Miller and the 1953 Social Science Research Council seminar); the cognitive line draws on Noam Chomsky, Jean Piaget, and Lev Vygotsky

name: Reduced Social Cues Approach
aka: Lack of Social Context Cues Theory
summary: When a medium strips away tone, face, and status, communication turns more equal but also blunter, colder, and more prone to flaming.
originator: Sara Kiesler, Jane Siegel, and Timothy McGuire; Lee Sproull and Sara Kiesler (the umbrella label "cues-filtered-out" was coined by Mary Culnan and M. Lynne Markus)

name: Semiotic Theories (Semiotics)
summary: The study of how signs carry meaning, treating words, images, gestures, and objects as bundles of form and concept whose link is held in place by social convention rather than nature.
originator: Ferdinand de Saussure and Charles Sanders Peirce (independently), with later cultural extension by Roland Barthes
year: Early 20th century (Saussure's Course in General Linguistics, 1916; Peirce's writings from the 1860s onward)

name: Social Cognitive Theory
aka: Social Cognitive Theory of Mass Communication
summary: People learn not only by doing but by watching others, acquiring new behaviors through observation, modeling, and a judgment about whether they can pull it off.
originator: Albert Bandura
year: 1977 (as Social Learning Theory); reformulated as Social Cognitive Theory in 1986

name: Social Constructionism (Social Construction of Reality)
summary: Reality as we experience it is not simply discovered but built and held in place through everyday interaction, shared habit, and the language a community uses to name its world.
originator: Peter L. Berger and Thomas Luckmann

name: Social Exchange Theory
summary: People build and keep relationships by weighing rewards against costs, staying when the payoff beats what they expect and what they could get elsewhere.
originator: John Thibaut and Harold Kelley; George C. Homans; Peter Blau

name: Social Identity Model of Deindividuation Effects (SIDE)
summary: Anonymity in a group does not dissolve the self into chaos; it can sharpen a shared social identity and tighten conformity to the group's norms.
originator: Stephen Reicher, Russell Spears, and Tom Postmes (building on earlier work by Martin Lea and Russell Spears)

name: Social Identity Theory
aka: Tajfel and Turner's Social Identity Theory
summary: A theory that explains how the groups people belong to become part of who they are, driving them to favor their own kind and define themselves against others.
originator: Henri Tajfel and John Turner

name: Social Information Processing Theory
aka: Social Information Processing Theory of CMC
summary: Online relationships can grow as warm and intimate as face-to-face ones; people just need more time to do it through words alone.
originator: Joseph B. Walther

name: Social Presence Theory
summary: A theory holding that communication media differ in how vividly they convey the felt presence of another person, and that this sense of "being with" someone shapes how warm and effective an exchange becomes.
originator: John Short, Ederyn Williams, and Bruce Christie

name: Social Support
summary: The study of how the resources people exchange through communication, from a comforting word to concrete help, protect well-being and help them cope with stress.
originator: Sidney Cobb and James S. House (foundational definitions); Terrance L. Albrecht and Mara B. Adelman (communication reframing)

name: Speech Act Theory
summary: When we speak we are not just describing the world, we are doing things in it: promising, warning, ordering, apologizing.
originator: J.L. Austin, extended and systematized by John R. Searle

name: Spiral of Silence
summary: People who sense their view is losing ground fall silent, and that silence makes the dominant view look even stronger, spinning opinion toward one side.
originator: Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann

name: System Theory
summary: The idea that an organization, a family, or a media ecosystem is best understood not as a pile of separate parts but as a living whole, where every element is tied to every other and the system behaves in ways no single part can explain.
originator: Ludwig von Bertalanffy (general system theory), extended to organizations by Daniel Katz and Robert Kahn

name: Theory of Planned Behavior
summary: A theory holding that behavior follows from intention, which is itself driven by our attitudes, the social pressure we feel, and how much control we believe we have.
originator: Icek Ajzen (building on the Theory of Reasoned Action with Martin Fishbein)

name: Transactional Model of Stress and Coping
aka: Transactional Theory of Stress and Coping
Lazarus and Folkman Stress and Coping Model
summary: Stress is not in the event itself but in the bargain a person strikes between what a situation demands and what they believe they can do about it.
originator: Richard S. Lazarus and Susan Folkman

name: Two-Step Flow
summary: Media messages rarely move the public directly; they pass first to engaged opinion leaders, who then relay and reshape them for everyone else.
originator: Paul F. Lazarsfeld, Bernard Berelson, and Hazel Gaudet (1944); developed with Elihu Katz (1955)

name: Uncertainty Reduction Theory
summary: When strangers meet, the drive to reduce uncertainty about each other powers the communication that turns acquaintances into relationships.
originator: Charles R. Berger and Richard J. Calabrese

name: Uses and Gratifications
summary: A theory that flips the usual question, asking not what media do to people but what people actively do with media to satisfy their own needs.
originator: Elihu Katz, Jay G. Blumler, and Michael Gurevitch (building on Herta Herzog's earlier audience studies)
